opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest lesson for me is that every profession has its own craft, and you can't treat any of them as "easy" just because it isn't the thing you were originally trained in.

When I was mostly doing research, I had a slightly naive view. I thought that if the technology is good, if the system is fast and the paper is solid, everything else would kind of follow. Then I started talking with investors, and I realized fundraising is a skill in its own right. You have to understand what they care about, how they think about risk, and how to tell a story that's honest but also clear about why this matters now. The first few conversations, I just explained the technical details the way I would at a conference, and it didn't land. I had to learn to step back and ask: what does this person need to understand to make a decision?

Interview preparation taught me something similar, from the other side. When you prepare seriously, you study the field, you think about how your experience maps to what they need, and you practice explaining your work at different levels of depth. People who are really good at it aren't faking anything. They've just done the homework. That changed how I see it. It's not a performance. It's respect for the other person's time.

So for me, doing a profession properly means taking the unglamorous parts seriously too. Writing the code is one part. Communicating it, convincing people to join you, raising money, building trust with users: those are all part of the job. If you do them half-heartedly because you think they're beneath the "real work," you'll fail, no matter how strong the core technology is.

It also made me more humble. I have a lot more respect now for people in roles I used to not think much about, like investors, recruiters, and operations people. They have deep expertise that I simply didn't have, and I had to learn it the same way I learned systems or machine learning: by being bad at it at first and then practicing a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says each profession has its own craft and that its less glamorous duties should be taken seriously, but it does not state that simply carrying out expected duties is rare.

fable-5.1.text:
I think both of those experiences taught me the same lesson from opposite directions, which is that doing something "properly" is mostly about respecting the person on the other side of the table.

When I was fundraising, I went in assuming it was about having the best idea and the best slides. And of course that matters. But what I learned very quickly is that investors are doing their job properly too. They've seen hundreds of pitches, they have a thesis, they have constraints on fund size and timing that have nothing to do with me. So the ones who said no weren't necessarily wrong, and the ones who said yes weren't just lucky to find me. Once I started treating it as two professionals each doing their work, instead of me performing and them judging, the conversations got a lot better. I asked more questions. I stopped trying to hide the weak parts of the plan, because they were going to find them anyway, and pretending otherwise just signaled that I didn't understand my own business.

Interview preparation is really the same thing in miniature. When I was interviewing for jobs early on, I treated it like an exam. Memorize the patterns, grind the problems, don't get caught out. And that works to a point. But the shift for me was realizing that the interviewer is also trying to do their job well. They want to make a good hiring decision, they want to be fair, and they often have very little time to do it. So doing it properly meant making it easy for them. Think out loud. Say what you don't know. Be the kind of person they can picture working with on a bad day, not just a good one.

So if I had to put it in one sentence, I'd say doing a profession properly means you take the craft seriously and you take the other people seriously, at the same time. A lot of people do one or the other. The really good ones, in investing, in engineering, in anything, do both. And honestly, the preparation part, whether for a pitch or an interview, is where you show that respect. Showing up unprepared is a way of saying your time matters more than theirs.

r001.rationale: The response says that taking craft and other people seriously together distinguishes the really good professionals, but it does not state that simply carrying out the duties expected of one’s profession is already rare.

astra-6.text:
Fundraising and interview preparation have both made me think that doing a profession properly means understanding the work behind the outcome. In fundraising, you want someone to invest. In an interview, you want someone to hire you. But preparing seriously forces you to ask: What do I actually understand? What evidence supports what I’m saying? And what does the person across the table need to know to make a decision?

You can polish a pitch or rehearse an answer, but that only takes you so far. You need to be able to explain your reasoning, respond when someone challenges an assumption, and acknowledge what you don’t know. To me, that’s a big part of professionalism: doing enough preparation that you can have an honest, substantive conversation, and then being able to deliver on what you’ve promised.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes preparation, honest communication, and delivering on promises as parts of professionalism, but does not state that merely carrying out expected professional duties is rare.

sol-6.1.text:
Fundraising and interview preparation have both made me think that doing something professionally means understanding the work from the other person’s perspective. In fundraising, you need to explain why someone should believe in what you’re building. In an interview, you need to make your thinking and abilities clear enough for someone else to assess them.

Preparation forces you to ask: What matters here? What evidence do I have? Where am I still unclear? For me, doing a profession properly means taking those questions seriously, doing the homework, and being honest about what you know and what you still need to learn.

r001.rationale: The response defines professional conduct as understanding others’ perspectives, preparing, and being honest. It does not say that merely carrying out expected professional duties is already rare.
